cells.tense: The work is on the bench and the hands are on it now.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: In the next session, carry your own share the whole way: finish the set, the page, the run you planned, without handing any part off or stopping early.
cells.core:
When the practice and the effort line up, you can stay at it long past the point where a burst would have quit. Repetition isn't a grind here — it's how something gets made. The hundredth pass isn't the same as the first, and somebody still has to do the hundredth. That steady staying is the whole advantage.

Keep it going by holding the middle of the work yourself, once. No shortcuts, no finishing loose, no letting the last part of a session drift because the beginning went well. If this isn't actually how you work, you've still spent one session fully inside it, and that teaches you something either way. The point isn't to prove anything. It's to know, from inside, that you can carry a whole piece to its end and stand on the result.
cells.sheetLine: The hundredth pass isn't the first, and it still counts.
cells.verb: finishing what sustained attention has been building
cells.place: at the small repeated practice, kept by showing up rather than by flashes

cells.tense: The final form is being forced into place before the work has had time to become it.
cells.ask: Sit for two minutes before the next session with empty hands and nothing to produce, letting whatever shows up show up, deciding nothing about it.
cells.core:
In the practice, the finish keeps getting pushed in front of the making. The form closes early, the last version gets rehearsed before it exists, and the work is being finished in your head faster than your hands can catch up. The grip is strong enough that nothing unexpected gets in, which means nothing new gets in either.

Open first, and start the session before you've decided what it will be. Two minutes, empty hands, nothing to make. Not a technique and not a break — a small window where the material can arrive without being summoned. Whatever comes, you don't have to act on it. If this read is off, you've still stood in one unforced minute, and that minute might save the session from being a rehearsal of its own blueprint.
cells.sheetLine: You finish the work before it's made, and nothing new reaches it.

cells.tense: The practice was left at a point that is already behind, and it has not been picked back up.
cells.act: see the thing as if for the first time
cells.ask: Take one small piece of the practice, do it once this week slowly, and look at it as though you were new to that piece, taking in what's there instead of labelling it.
cells.core:
The bench is there and the hands are not. Somewhere the practice stopped being continued and became remembered. It might have gone well and you stepped away without deciding to, or it stopped mattering and that hasn't been said. Either way, the outward form of it isn't moving, and the absence is easier not to look at than to look at.

Don't push effort back into it. Just look. One small piece, done once, slowly, without the old labels for it. Seeing is what comes back first, and the practice follows seeing rather than the other way around. If this doesn't match what's going on, a single unhurried look at some part of the work asks almost nothing of you and is yours whatever the reason it stopped.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped carrying it, and haven't looked at that.

cells.tense: The practice runs on without the one doing it having claimed it.
cells.act: describe what is in front of your eyes in five plain lines, no conclusions
cells.ask: At the start of the next session, describe the plain setup there in five flat lines — tools, space, page — saying what's present and drawing nothing from it.
cells.core:
You keep the practice going, and in your telling of your own life it isn't really yours — it's what you do, not something you built. The repetition quietly made you better at this, and no one signed it. You'd call it habit if asked, and you wouldn't be lying, exactly.

Look before you name anything, once. Five plain lines about what's actually on the bench at the start of the next session — the tools, the light, the page. No verdict in any of them. That's the oldest and simplest form of the same seeing that has kept this practice lit, and it belongs to whoever is doing it. Which is, whatever the account says, you. Nothing needs concluding for that to hold.
cells.sheetLine: Your hands built it, and your account says it happened anyway.

Reader's likely objection: 'I don't have a legacy or a body of work,' which is fine — the cells name what the capacity is doing right now, not what has been produced. The ask survives a wrong read in all four cells because each one asks for a single visible run at the practice, not a verdict on the person.
